title: MoE-Spec: Expert Budgeting for Efficient Speculative Decoding. Bradley McDanel (Franklin & Marshall; Meta Reality Labs), Steven Li, Sruthikesh Surineni, Harshit Khaitan (Meta Reality Labs). Preprint, 19 Feb 2026 (arXiv header: 17 Feb 2026).
id_read: arXiv 2602.16052v1 (PDF, pdftotext raw, 964 lines; read fully except appendix figures)
setup: OLMoE-1B-7B (7B/1B active, 64 experts, top-8), Qwen3-30B-A3B (128 experts, top-8), Mixtral-8x7B (8 experts, top-2). Drafts: EAGLE-3 for OLMoE/Qwen3, EAGLE-1 for Mixtral. NVIDIA A100 80GB (Mixtral on 2 GPUs), FP16, PyTorch 2.1/CUDA 12.1, ALL experts GPU-resident (App. A Table 3). Single request, draft tree 63 tokens (sweep 3-511), 80 samples/benchmark, max 1024 new tokens, T=0 and T=1 (5 seeds). Benchmarks GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, CNN/DM. Baselines AR, EAGLE (named per model). Budget B chosen to maximise speed while quality stays within 1 std of EAGLE (budgets 8-56 OLMoE, 16-64 Qwen3, 2-7 Mixtral).

why: GPU-resident experts: the saving is HBM bandwidth over the verification union, not an NVMe read. Draft is a trained EAGLE head. Lossy truncation/substitution (we require exact routing). Trees of 63 tokens on 64-128-expert models; our chains are k=8 on 512 experts top-10. Their tail-dropping idea (93% of mass in top half of experts) is a lossy route-restriction lever which does match the family of 'restrict the union' but without any cache term. Authors note batched serving would see smaller gains.
quality_loss: Lossy by construction (experts outside the shortlist are dropped or substituted). Table 1 picks the budget within 1 std of EAGLE quality, so table accuracies are close (e.g. Qwen3 HumanEval T=0 78 vs 82 AR, 82 EAGLE-3; Mixtral HumanEval 27 vs 20 AR, noise-level). Tighter budgets: Fig 3 quality relative to AR falls to ~78% (Mixtral) at maximum speedup; Static ranking gives near-zero GSM8K/MATH500 accuracy at B<=16 (Fig 5a); Router ranking tracks an oracle; Oracle reaches near-AR quality at B=24 (37.5% of experts).
ablation: Yes, Sec 4.4: ranking method (static/router/oracle) and coverage policy (truncation vs substitution perform comparably); tree-size sweep; reconstruction error (Fig 6: oracle matches router with 25% fewer experts). No ablation against any cache/offload.
limitations: Authors (Sec 6): budget hyperparameter must be chosen per deployment; router-based ranking adds 2-3% overhead and may not pay for very small trees; single-request A100 only, batching may give smaller gains; softmax routing only (DeepSeek-V3 sigmoid may need adaptation); no per-layer budget; no co-activation model.
contradicts_our_findings: No. Fig 4a shows the union approaches all experts for big trees (EAGLE-3 54 of 64 at tree 255), consistent with our measured union 29.1 of 64 (45%) at k=8 on the 128-expert trace. Their finding that EAGLE speedup peaks then declines with tree size (1.95x -> 1.85x) matches our 'union cost eats acceptance gain'. Nothing about an LRU cache or disk.

why: HBM-bound 8xH200 with experts resident; no offloading, no SSD, no CPU. Needs a trained per-model predictor and a trained draft (EAGLE-3/MTP). Gains come from picking 4 verified nodes with overlapping experts; with gamma=4 the union is only 20.5 experts/layer. In our regime the extra cost term would be a disk read, which the paper never models; the draft-selection idea (choose tree nodes whose predicted experts are already resident) is transferable in principle, the numbers are not. Batch >1 shows the gain shrinks and goes negative (0.65-0.69x at batch 8).
quality_loss: None claimed (verification rule unchanged, lossless draft-tree selection); acceptance length drops slightly (2.41 -> 2.32 Qwen3).
ablation: Table 4: static global-cost vs dynamic marginal-cost scoring; Table 9: predictor accuracy 50%/60%/converged (1.17/1.29/1.39x GSM8K Qwen3); Table 10: oracle vs predicted expert sets are identical (20.4 vs 20.5 experts). No cache/offload ablation.
limitations: No dedicated limitations section. Prototype on HF Transformers; DeepSeek-V3.1 gains small because routing is balanced (App D); speedups fall with batch.
contradicts_our_findings: Internal inconsistency: Table 3 latencies (AR 0.490 s/token, EAGLE-3 0.840 s/step with 2.41 accepted tokens) imply 0.49*2.41/0.84 = 1.41x for EAGLE-3 and 1.53x for EcoSpec on Qwen3, but the same table and Table 1 report 1.22x and 1.36x; GPT-OSS: 1.03x/1.17x implied vs 1.14x/1.31x reported; so the AR time or the speedup basis is not the one stated. Does not contradict our measurements; Table 8 (verification of 4 tokens costs 1.1-1.7x an AR step even on H200) supports 'verify is not free on MoE'.

MoE-SpeQ is lossless but its cache is 16-32 GB for 15-42B models (~50-100% of experts), unlike our 4%-12% cache share. The prefetch lever is the part relevant to us; its isolated ablation in MoE-SpeQ is small (5%).

limitations: SP-MoE (Sec 7): batch size 1 only (large batches uncorrelated expert activation left to future work), sequential greedy drafting only, no tree or sampling. MoE-SpeQ v1: cannot ablate a dense draft as no matched small MoEs exist; compared only with Transformers-based baselines (llama.cpp/vLLM infeasible in v1).
contradicts_our_findings: No direct contradiction. SP-MoE's own text: with longer drafts the number of required experts grows and 'reaching full-expert activation increases loading overhead', performance gaps narrow (Fig 13) - same mechanism as our union growth.

setup: OLMoE-1B-7B (6.7B total, 64 experts top-8), DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (15.3B, 64 top-6), Qwen3-30B-A3B (30.5B, 128 top-8), GPT-OSS-120B (116.8B, 128 experts top-4). Implemented in llama.cpp with a new expert-level offload (non-expert params resident; frequently used experts kept resident from offline profiling; no LRU/prefetch baseline because none exists for llama.cpp). Training-free; components: routing-aware adaptive expansion (utility = confidence*T_AR / (marginal new experts*T_exp + draft cost)), reuse-aware expert gating (additive logit bias toward experts shared across draft tokens: LOSSY), context-aligned draft sharing the target KV cache. Tasks: Spec-Bench categories MT, RG, SU, TR, QA, MA (math), HE.

ablation: Fig 8 progressive speedup (self-spec + context alignment + adaptive expansion + reuse-aware gating); Fig 9 expansion strategies; Tables 3-4 context alignment and expert reuse; Fig 10 sensitivity to draft top-k and reuse cap. The cache-vs-layout-vs-prefetch decomposition is absent (no cache baseline).
limitations: No limitation section. Authors state gating is not strictly lossless; evaluation only Jetson + one 4090; no comparison with any caching/prefetch offloader (none in llama.cpp).
contradicts_our_findings: Does not contradict the lossless byte arithmetic, but it is a counter-example to 'speculation cannot pay on an SSD-bound llama.cpp path': 1.3-5.3x on SSD-bound Jetson. Reason it can differ from ours: (a) lossy gating cuts the union, (b) baseline has no cache, (c) acceptance lengths 5-7 (OLMoE) imply a >85% per-token acceptance for the draft, above our modelled 0.5-0.9 and tied to a specific self-draft. Also AR rates are tiny (0.47-0.95 tok/s for 30B-120B at 16GB), consistent with our 8GB/NVMe order of magnitude.
